newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: E.Europe coffee markets retain growth potential.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe coffee markets retain growth potential.

text.p: Coffee consumption in Eastern Europe has grown steadily over the past five years and the region is still seen as a key future market for the industry to develop, according to a new study.

But the 10-page report by Hasso Kaempfe, President of the German Coffee Association and a board member of top German roaster Tchibo, said growth in the former Soviet states had not been as rapid as earlier anticipated.

"At the time (of political change) there was a keen interest in Western brands while at the same time local products were of inferior quality," he said in his report, released at the end of a three-day International Tea and Coffee Symposium conference in Vienna last week.
But he added, "Volume development has been very disappointing. We had to discover...that the expected growth was largely an illusion."
The report said the sharp rise in world coffee prices in 1994 together with the impact of the implementation of tough economic reforms were the main reasons for seeing slower growth rates.
"The precipitate rise in prices for raw coffee in 1994 had, of course, a particularly strong effect on Central and Eastern Europe," said the report.

"But even without this surprise effect the financial means for buying the luxury product coffee were much more restricted than was expected, the culprit being the gradual curtailing of subventions for basic food, rents and energy.

"As a consequence, the per capita consumption has not changed much since 1991/92," Kaempfe said, describing Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic as "the three most important markets" in Eastern Europe.
According to the figures presented in the report, roasted coffee consumption in Poland rose to 69,000 tonnes in 1996 from 57,000 tonnes in 1992, and was expected to climb to 72,000 tonnes in 1997.

Hungary saw its coffee consumption increasing to 23,000 tonnes in 1993, up from 20,000 tonnes in 1992, but saw consumption declining again to 20,000 tonnes in 1996. A slight increase to 21,000 tonnes was expected for 1997.
The Czech Republic went gradually from a 16,500-tonne consumption figure in 1992 to 17,500-tonnes in 1996, a figure which was forecast to further jump to 18,500 tonnes this year.

Kaempfe warned investors to look into several local factors if they wanted to enter the Eastern European markets successfully, and in particular pointed to high import duties on roasted coffee in Poland and Hungary.
"Despite the large size of each market a production plant has to be established in each individual country as a consequence of the high import costs," he said.

He also said the consumers in the former communist countries, which have an average per capita consumption of below 2.0 kg of coffee per year compared to some 4.2 kg in Western Europe, had "turned out to be quite conservative".

"It is also interesting to see that the obsolete brand denominations which had been used by all Czech roasting establishments in former times....are still so thoroughly engraved in people's minds that all international companies have included these denominations in their respective product range.
"An individual blend and packaging concept is necessary for each country," said Kaempfe.
He said long-term prospects pointed to the "possibility that the new markets in Central and Eastern Europe will contribute to a growth of world wide coffee consumption ...".
"Especially Russia, the Baltic states and the Balkan states are attractive on a long-term scale and big companies are already working on these markets, but their volumes are as of yet negligible.

"In all these countries, and especially in the Czech Republic and in Hungary, there are long-standing coffee traditions which would make a much higher per capita consumption possible than is the case today.

"A per capita consumption of 3.0 kilogrammes, which is rather moderate when compared to the European average, translates to a market growth of 50 percent -- an enticing prospect in any case," Kaempfe said.
